segments.narration: A rotted ship left a perfect outline in the sand. Suffolk, 1939. Twenty-seven metres of oak, gone, every iron rivet still in place.
Inside it: a war helmet in hundreds of pieces, gold and garnet shoulder clasps, ten nested silver bowls, a lyre, and a purse of thirty-seven gold coins.
Every one of those coins came from a different Frankish mint. Someone was buried here like a king. Except there was no body.
Soil tests did find phosphate, the trace a body leaves. The usual explanation is acid sand that ate the bone; some argue nobody was buried there.
The coins date the grave to between 610 and 635. Most scholars think the man in that ship was Raedwald, king of the East Angles.

verdicts.claim: The Sutton Hoo ship burial, excavated in 1939, contained a ship about 27 metres long whose timber had decayed, leaving its shape preserved in the sand with nearly all its iron rivets in place.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives the ship as about 27 m long and 4.4 m wide, states the timber had decayed but the sand preserved its shape with nearly all iron rivets in place, and dates the Mound 1 excavation to May 1939.

verdicts.claim: The burial held a ceremonial helmet reassembled from hundreds of fragments, gold-and-garnet shoulder clasps, ten nested silver bowls, a lyre and a purse of 37 gold coins.
verdicts.note: All five items are listed in Wikipedia's account of the Mound 1 finds, including the helmet shattered in the collapse and reassembled from hundreds of fragments.

verdicts.claim: Each of the 37 gold coins in the purse came from a different Frankish mint.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia describes a purse containing 37 gold coins, each from a different Frankish mint.

verdicts.claim: No skeleton survived in the burial chamber, but soil analysis found phosphate traces suggesting a body once lay there, and some scholars argue the ship was a cenotaph.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia states no skeleton survived, that soil analysis found phosphate traces suggesting a body once lay there, and that some scholars have proposed the ship was a cenotaph. The narration presents acid soil as the usual explanation rather than settled fact, which matches the source's framing.

verdicts.claim: Coin analysis narrows the burial to between 610 and 635, and most scholars favour Raedwald, king of the East Angles, who died around 624.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia cites Gareth Williams's coin analysis narrowing the burial to 610-635 and states most scholars favour Raedwald, king of the East Angles, who died around 624.
